title: Plague years
hook: during the plague, he fled his home with his family and admired the calm of peasants facing death (Essays 3.12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, of cripples, and your line was not so sure. Did a harsh verdict soften into a perhaps? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

The plague reached the country around Montaigne's house. He writes about it in book three, in an essay called Of physiognomy. He gathered his family and left home, looking for somewhere safe to stay. It wasn't easy. A family fleeing the plague frightened the people they hoped would take them in. Friends grew wary; hosts grew nervous at any sign of illness. The man who wrote so calmly about death in his tower now had to face it on the road, with his household behind him. And what he noticed most, he says, was not the scholars. It was the farmers.
screen: `THE PLAGUE COMES CLOSE.` → `A FAMILY ON THE ROAD.` → `HE WATCHES THE FARMERS.`

segments.voice: First, what he saw. The country people around him, Montaigne writes, faced the sickness with a plainness that stunned him. He says the grapes were left hanging on the vines, as people readied themselves for death without drama. He tells of a man, still in good health, who was already digging his own grave, and of others who lay down in theirs while still alive. Grim pictures. But what struck him was the quiet in them. Second, calm without books. Here's the turn. Montaigne had spent a long time reading philosophers on how to prepare for death. And these people, who had read none of it, met death more steadily than the learned. He doesn't romanticize their hardship. He's simply honest that their calm wasn't borrowed from a library. Third, nature as teacher. He writes, roughly, that if you don't know how to die, don't worry; nature will teach you fully when the moment comes. And he adds a line that turns the whole thing around: we trouble our life with worry about death, and our death with worry about life. Fourth, plain and brave. The essay's title points to faces, and Montaigne spends much of it on Socrates, whose face was plain, even ugly by his account, and whose courage was not. The farmers and Socrates belong together in his mind: no show, no speech, just steadiness. In daily life, the bravest person you know may not be the loudest. Look for the one who simply keeps going.
screen: `THEY FACED IT PLAINLY.` · `CALM WITHOUT A LIBRARY.` · `NATURE WILL TEACH YOU.` · `PLAIN FACES, STEADY HEARTS.` · then, large: `THE PEASANTS' CALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from someone plain and brave. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who carried something hard without making a show of it: a grandparent, a nurse, a neighbor, a friend who kept going through an illness or a loss. Remember one ordinary thing they did in the middle of it. Making tea. Going to work. Telling a joke. Let that small, steady act be your teacher for these minutes. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Plague years. Montaigne on the road, learning steadiness from people who had read none of the books he had. Today's word.

Your line: the peasants' calm. Today, thank one plain, brave person, aloud or in your head. And that closes a week with Montaigne: the whole human condition, steady change, three companies, a new route, two not one, not so sure, and the peasants' calm. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of physiognomy often remember his account of the plague, and his admiration for country people who met death with a calm no book had taught them.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne, the plague is close, and you've read the philosophers on death. who teaches you most?
fork.reveal: the country people, who met death plainly without the books, struck him more than anything he'd read.

trapdoor: what you thought: an essay called Of physiognomy is about reading faces.
what it means: it is about plain people, and a plain-faced philosopher, whose courage needs no show.
what a scholar hears: Montaigne sets the farmers beside Socrates, whose plain face hid a fine soul.
